label: Perturbation Theory
notes: Open by framing the appendix as the place where the dream of integrability meets its limits. We start from an integrable system in action-angle form and ask what survives a small Hamiltonian perturbation. Preview the three landmarks: the homological equation, small denominators, and the verdicts of Poincare, KAM, and Nekhoroshev.

label: Integrable Background
notes: Remind students that action-angle variables turn an integrable Hamiltonian into a function of the actions alone. The angles wind uniformly with frequencies given by the gradient of H zero. Each torus is invariant, and the whole phase space foliates into these tori. This clean picture is exactly what the perturbation will threaten.

label: The Perturbed Problem
notes: Introduce the perturbed Hamiltonian and the central goal: find a canonical change of variables that pushes the angle dependence to higher order in epsilon. Stress that we are not solving the system, only trying to make it look integrable order by order. The generating function is the unknown we expand in powers of epsilon.

label: Generating Function Scheme
notes: Walk through the near-identity canonical transformation built from a generating function of mixed old and new variables. Expanding everything in epsilon and matching the first order gives a single linear equation for S one. Emphasize that the structure repeats at every order, so understanding order one tells the whole story.

label: The Homological Equation
notes: Derive the homological equation: the directional derivative of S one along the unperturbed flow must cancel the oscillating part of H one. This is the heart of perturbation theory. It is a transport equation along the linear winding of the torus, and its solvability depends entirely on the arithmetic of the frequencies.

label: Fourier Solution
notes: Solve the homological equation by Fourier series on the torus. Each Fourier mode of the perturbation divides by the inner product of the integer vector k with the frequency vector omega. Point out the zero mode constraint: the average of H one shifts the new Hamiltonian and cannot be removed, defining the corrected frequencies.

label: Small Denominators
notes: This is the crisis slide. The denominators k dot omega can be made arbitrarily small by suitable integer vectors, since rationally related frequencies make them vanish exactly. Even tiny Fourier coefficients are amplified without bound. Use the plot to show the denominator dipping toward zero on resonance lines, blowing the series coefficients up.

label: Resonances in Action Space
notes: Move from a single torus to the whole action space. Each resonance condition k dot omega equals zero is a hypersurface, and together they form a dense web. Near this web the construction fails, while in the non-resonant complement it has a chance. The picture is a fractured plane of resonance lines over surviving regions.

label: Divergence and Poincare
notes: State the bad news plainly. The naive series generally diverges because the resonance web is dense, so no neighborhood is free of small denominators. Connect this to Poincare's theorem: for a generic perturbation there are no analytic first integrals independent of the energy. Integrability is destroyed by the perturbation in the analytic category.

label: Diophantine Frequencies
notes: Introduce the rescue. Frequencies satisfying a Diophantine condition stay quantitatively far from resonance, so the denominators decay only polynomially in the mode index. This controlled lower bound is precisely what convergence proofs need. Note that almost every frequency vector is Diophantine, even though the bad set is dense.

label: The KAM Theorem
notes: Present KAM as the triumph over small denominators. Under a nondegeneracy condition and sufficiently small epsilon, tori with Diophantine frequencies survive, merely deformed. The invariant tori fill a set of large measure, while resonant gaps host chaos. Mention the rapidly convergent Newton scheme that defeats the divergence of the naive series.

label: Nekhoroshev and Recap
notes: Close with Nekhoroshev's exponential stability: even where tori break, actions drift only by tiny amounts over times exponentially long in one over epsilon. Recap the arc from homological equation to small denominators to the KAM and Nekhoroshev resolutions, and stress that arithmetic of frequencies governs the fate of motion.
